<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
I'll add drag-to-scroll to the Collection badges.

Native touch scrolling and mouse drag will handle horizontal scrolling with a grab cursor. Scrollbars stay hidden. A negative margin will create a full-bleed effect. A small peek of the next badge will signal scrollability.

Scroll-snap will align badges to the grid. Dragging temporarily disables snap and hides text selection. The badge grid uses a flex layout with fixed gaps.

Badge widths will be calculated as a percentage of the scroller viewport rather than using fixed pixel values. This keeps the layout responsive and avoids issues with max-content sizing.

Percentage widths for badges fail when the flex container uses max-content, since the percentage would depend on the container's own size. A different sizing strategy is needed.

Container queries fix the circular width problem. The scroller gets `container-type: inline-size`, and each badge uses `calc((100cqi - 1.412rem) / 3.15)` to size itself against the visible viewport. A fixed `7.2rem` fallback handles browsers that do not support container queries.

The scroller viewport is roughly 330 pixels wide after subtracting screen and collection padding. Three badges plus gaps would leave about 102 pixels per badge. A slightly smaller width of around 97 pixels is better for a clear peek of the next badge. Two to three badges with a visible edge will signal scrollability cleanly.

The Collection section itself will lose its overflow scroll so only the badge row scrolls. The pointer drag logic captures the starting position and scroll offset, then calculates horizontal movement to drive the scroll.

The drag logic ignores touch input to prevent double-scrolling with native touch scrolling. Only mouse drag will drive the scroll. The gesture is meant to feel like holding and sliding the badges directly.

The scroller will use `touch-action: pan-x` to allow horizontal panning without interfering with vertical page scrolling. The home screen itself will stay locked with `overflow: hidden`, so only the badge row scrolls. The collection section will drop its vertical overflow, leaving the badge grid as the sole scroller. Shorter badges will not trigger a vertical scrollbar because the collection area is flexible.

A flex-1 badge grid would fill the card vertically, but the current two-row layout uses more vertical space. Short badges would leave sparse blue gaps below, so the existing layout is preferable.

The collection card will become a flex column so the badge row fills the remaining height. The scroller will use flex: 1 to stretch across the card, while the badge grid and its items will be set to 100% height. This makes the badges fill the vertical space and scroll horizontally within the card.

Badges will use a 5:8 aspect ratio. Images will fill the article height minus the label, with width set automatically by the aspect ratio. The badge cards will be centered vertically inside the flex column.

Portrait phones will show roughly two and a half badges with a visible edge. On taller screens the badges grow and fewer fit, yet they remain scrollable.
</details></think>

The scroller switches to a grabbing cursor while dragging and disables scroll snapping during movement. The badge grid stretches to full height and uses a flex layout with small gaps. Badge labels get tight margins and ellipsis overflow. Images and mystery placeholders use aspect-ratio 5/8 with flexible sizing. A width-height dependency issue is surfacing where the article width is driven by content, the image height by the article, and the image width by its own height.

The Collection card is 321 pixels tall on a 390 by 844 pixel phone.

The badge scroller is 265 pixels tall, but the badges are only 160 pixels tall and start 52 pixels from the top. This leaves a lot of empty blue space. Badges are currently sized by width divided by 3.4 instead of by available height. A better approach is to size badges to fill the scroller height. If they still do not fit, the container scrolls. Otherwise they simply sit there.

Filling the scroller height yields roughly 160-pixel-wide badges. On mobile, three badges would fit with a slight peek, creating a strong scroll. On desktop, three badges would fit almost exactly. This confirms the correct sizing model.

The implementation uses flexbox stretching. The grid and its articles stretch to fill the scroller height. Images and mystery elements flex to fill remaining space while keeping their aspect ratio. This makes badges fill the row vertically without scrollbars.

The flexbox approach proved unreliable. A more dependable method uses a container query on the scroller. The container gets `container-type: size`. Each badge article then sets its height to 100% and derives its width with `calc((100cqh - 1.15rem) * 494 / 743)`. This ties badge dimensions directly to the scroller height.

The scroller has a definite height because it uses flex 1 and min-height 0. On a 265-pixel scroller, subtracting the label space of 19.5 pixels leaves about 245.5 pixels for the image. At the 494-to-743 aspect ratio, that yields a width of roughly 163 pixels. The article itself should stay at 100% height, letting the image fill the remaining vertical space.

The formula now subtracts 1.35rem for the label, yielding roughly 163 pixels on mobile and 118 pixels on desktop. This keeps the image height near the scroller edge, leaving a tight but usable scroll. A maximum width will prevent badges from becoming oversized on taller containers.

The container query will use `container-type: size` rather than `inline-size` so `cqh` resolves correctly. The scroller’s height comes from flex, not its children, so size containment should not collapse it. The old 3.4 flex basis will be removed. Images and mystery elements will stretch to fill

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
The build fails because `el` is a `const` assigned from `scrollerRef`, so TypeScript treats it as possibly null.

TypeScript does not preserve the null narrowing from the early return inside nested functions. Because `el` is a `const` assigned from a nullable ref, the compiler assumes the closure could be invoked later while `el` is still null.

The fix is to reassign `el` to a new `const` after the null guard. This preserves the narrowed type inside the nested function.

The cleanest fix is to declare a new `const` with an explicit `HTMLDivElement` type right after the null guard. This gives TypeScript a fresh non-null binding inside the nested function. A non-null assertion would work but is less precise. I will apply the fix and rebuild.
</details></think>
